@@50073589 <h> Opinion We must strengthen environmental protections during drought -- or face irreversible loss <p> Australian wildlife can generally cope with drought , but they 're not prepared for the combination of people , introduced animals , and no water . <p> Sheep with lambs in north west NSW , Australia , during the 2018 drought . Image from Shutterstock <p> Australian rural communities face hardships during extended drought , and it is generally appropriate that governments then provide special support for affected landholders and communities . <p> However , some politicians and commentators have recently claimed that such circumstances should be addressed by circumventing environmental laws or management -- by , for example , reallocating environmental water to grow fodder or opening up conservation reserves for livestock grazing . <p> But subverting or weakening existing protective conservation management practices and policies will exacerbate the impacts of drought on natural environments and biodiversity . <h> Drought-related decline in wildlife <p> Impacts of severe weather on some natural systems are obvious and well-recognised . For example , during periods of elevated sea temperature , coral bleaching may conspicuously signal extensive environmental degradation and biodiversity loss . <p> On land , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ natural systems may be less obvious , even if of comparable magnitude . <p> Nonetheless , the record is clear : drought leads to extensive and severe declines in many wildlife species . <p> Early observers in Australia reported the collapse of bird communities ( " the bush fell silent " ) and other wildlife across vast areas during the Federation Drought . <p> Unsurprisingly , wetland environments , and species dependent on them , may bear the brunt of impacts . That said , impacts are pervasive across all landscapes exposed to drought . <p> Drought contributed to the extinction of one of Australia 's most beautiful birds , the Paradise Parrot . For example , the pastoralist and zoologist Charles Barnard noted : <p> Previous to the terrible drought of 1902 it was not uncommon to see a pair of these birds when out mustering ... but since that year not a single specimen has been seen ... For three years ... there had been no wet season , and very little grass grew , consequently there was little seed ; then the worst year came on , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ could not find a living , and ... perished ... they have not found their way back . <p> Drought contributed to the extinction of one of Australia 's most beautiful birds , the Paradise Parrot . Wikimedia , CC BY <p> After the long droughts break , native plant and animal species may take many years to recover , and some never recover or return to their former range . <p> Threatened plant and animal species -- with an already tenuous toe-hold on existence -- are often the mostaffected . <p> Days of extremely hot temperatures also exceed the thermoregulatory tolerance of some species . That means mass mortality for some animals ; and large numbers of even hardy native trees may be killed by heat and lack of rain across extensive areas . <p> Furthermore , water sources can disappear from much of the landscape . Organisms dependent on floods are now more vulnerable , given that overallocation of water from rivers has increased drying of wetlands . <h> Drought is not new in Australia , but the stresses are greater now <p> Of course , drought has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many Australian plants and animals are among the most drought-adapted and resilient in the world . But drought impacts on wildlife are now likely to be of unprecedented severity and duration , for several reasons : <p> with global climate change , droughts will be more severe and frequent . There will be less opportunity for wildlife to recover in the reduced interval between drought periods <p> feral cats and introduced foxes now occur across most of Australia . In drought periods , these hunt more effectively because drought reduces the ground-layer vegetation that many native prey species rely upon for shelter . Cats and foxes also congregate and hunt more efficiently as wildlife cluster around the few water sources that are left <p> prior to European settlement , the reduction in vegetation during drought would have been accompanied by natural feedback loops , notably reduction in the density of native herbivores . Now , livestock are often maintained in drought-affected areas , with supplementary food provided , but they also graze on what little native vegetation remains . Now , wildlife must compete with feral goats , camels and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ native vegetation across much of the eastern rangelands means it will now be much harder for species lost from some areas during drought to recolonise their former haunts after drought . The habitat connectivity has been lost <p> many wildlife species could previously endure drought by maintaining a residue of their population in small refuge areas , where nutrients or moisture persisted in an otherwise hostile landscape . Now , livestock , feral herbivores and predators also congregate at these areas , making them less effective as native wildlife refuges <p> in at least woodland and forest habitats , droughts may interact with other factors . Notably , drought increases the likelihood of high intensity and extensive bushfires that can cause long-lasting damage to wildlife and environments . <p> Our intention here is not to downplay the needs or plight of rural communities affected by drought . <p> Rather , we seek to bring attention to the other life struggling in that landscape . Australia should bolster , not diminish , conservation efforts during drought times . If we do n't , we will suffer irretrievable losses to our nature @

@@50074106 <h> Scotland 's oldest heritage sites at risk from rising seas <p> Archaeologists are now quickly documenting sites built before Stonehenge and the pyramids before climate change erases them . <p> UpdatedUpdated 4 days ago <p> By Jim Dwyer 2018 New York Times <p> Share <p> Off the north coast of Scotland , Orkney 's soft green landscapes hold a trove of things from everyday life before history was written . <p> More than 3,000 archaeological sites -- among them standing stone circles , Norse halls and a Neolithic tomb graffitied by Vikings -- have endured for millenniums , scattered across the roughly 70 islands that make up the Orkney archipelago . <p> At Skara Brae , one of Europe 's best-preserved Stone Age villages , kitchens built around 3180 BC are fitted with hearths and cupboards , bedsteads and doors that could be bolted shut . <p> Today , in forays to remote spits of land , people are working to save some of these places for posterity from the climate changes accelerated by human activity . <p> About half of Orkney 's 3,000 sites , many built before Stonehenge or the pyramids , are under threat from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are already being washed away . <p> Since 1970 , Orkney beaches have eroded twice as fast as in the previous century . Others that had been stable are now shrinking . Rains , falling heavier and more often , are dissolving the crusts of soil and sand packs that protect remnants of civilizations . <p> Skara Brae , one of Europes best-preserved Stone Age villages , in the Orkney Islands in Scotland , July 28 , 2018 . <p> NYTNS <p> These threats , now familiar at world heritage sites around the globe , are being answered in Scotland by archaeologists , citizen-scientists , students , government agencies and academics . <p> Their work is urgent . Orkney 's stories are recorded in disappearing ink . <p> " Heritage is falling into the sea , " said Jane Downes , director of the Archaeology Institute at the University of Highlands and Islands . " It 's a very dramatic and obvious sign of sea level rise and increased storminess . " <p> From around the world , troops of archaeologists and students descend in the summers to dig , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ funds . " We 're focused on coastal sites because they 're going to be gone , " Downes said . <p> At many spots , the only plausible kind of preservation is documentation -- done swiftly . <p> In 1983 , an archaeologist drew sketches of a Neolithic chambered tomb at the tip of a peninsula on Sanday island . Then the site was left essentially untouched until last year , when other researchers returned , planning to deploy new tools that would tell them where the people of that area came from and what they ate . <p> But the tomb and its archaeology had shrunk : five feet had been lost to cliff erosion , and it was evident that the remaining 40 feet were headed for the water as well . <p> Skara Brae , one of Europes best-preserved Stone Age villages , in the Orkney Islands in Scotland , July 30 , 2018 . <p> NYTNS <p> At the end of the summer digging season , students packed the site with rock and a thick plastic membrane . Depending on the severity of the winter @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sediments from washing away , and also allow another year of excavation at the deteriorating tomb . <p> In a short walk along the south shore of Rousay Island , a stunning arc of human activity comes into view . One mile covers 50 centuries : the Stone , Bronze and Iron Ages . The Picts , the Viking era , rule by the Norse , and Scottish landlords . <p> The burial of a cow on Rousay in 1963 led to the discovery of human graves and , in them , evidence of long-distance travel . For instance , a silver brooch inlaid with amber and gold filigree from about 750 AD is similar to Irish jewellery of the era , said Julie Gibson , a lecturer with the University of Highlands and Islands and the co-author , with the photographer Frank Bradford , of " Rising Tides : The Loss of Coastal Heritage in Orkney . " <p> Nearby , in a Viking cemetery , Gibson said : " They found two guys buried in boats . One was born north of the Arctic Circle . " <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ built atop the homes of predecessors , creating layers of habitation back to Neolithic times . SWEEPER was shown thousands of pictures of peppers just to be able to identify the vegetables . " We think they would help with tasks that are difficult for people to do . " <p> The BGU team is developing other agricultural innovations too . @@50084329 <h> What Does Fuel Emissions and Consumption Really Mean ? <h> When fuel ignites inside an engine , some people think that an explosion occurs . <p> It might sound like semantics , but it is actually a controlled combustion -- the difference between throwing together ingredients for a dinner meal , and carefully measuring each one out . <p> Just as an engine knows how to blend the right quantities of fuel , air and spark , fuel companies are given the recipe that they must meet in order for their refineries to turn barrels of crude oil into an unleaded or diesel brew . In the red-hot shaking of hands between engine and fuel , good energy is made -- but bad emissions are also expunged via exhaust gases . <h> How do you find the fuel consumption and emission stats of your vehicle ? <p> What comes out of the tailpipe is the focus of Australian fuel consumption and carbon dioxide ( or CO2 -- the leading contributor to climate change ) testing , the results of which are published on a yellow , red and green sticker glued to the front of all new vehicles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ urban , extra urban and combined -- each in litres of fuel consumed per 100 kilometres ( L/100km ) , next to the number of grams of CO2 produced per kilometre . Because burning a litre of petrol or diesel equates to emitting 2.3kg and 2.7kg of CO2 respectively , these numbers are interlinked and the result forms a simple mathematical equation of those figures in kilograms multiplied by L/100km . <h> What Does Fuel Emissions and Consumption Really Mean ? <p> Unlike in Europe and other countries , Australia does not tax based on how much fuel an engine drinks and the CO2 it harms the planet with . It means that a Toyota Camry Hybrid can produce 111 grams of CO2 per kilometre , and HiLux diesel from the same brand can belch out twice that , at 223g/km of CO2 , without any emissions penalty . <p> What Australia does , however , is ( partially ) join Continental allies in capping other noxious emissions -- and whether it is a hybrid or diesel-guzzling Toyota , the exhaust gases must not exceed a certain limit . <h> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ consumption measurement is called the Australian Design Rules ( ADR ) 81/02 test and it is based on a decades old , and now-superseded New European Driving Cycle ( NEDC ) . <p> It places each vehicle on a rolling dynamometer in a laboratory for 20 minutes -- including a 13min ' urban ' simulation that spikes the vehicle from standstill to just under 20km/h , to standstill , to 30km/h , to standstill , to 50km/h and to standstill in four repetitions for a 19km/h average speed . Then it moves to a 7min ' extra urban ' cycle that accelerates to 70km/h , slows to 50km/h , speeds back to 70km/h then gradually to 100km/h and 120km/h , then to standstill for a 63km/h overall average speed . <p> While the combined figure is then averaged in a 66:34 split ( in urban 's favour ) , the Department of Transport and Infrastructure admits that the test can not simulate all ' real world ' conditions . <p> In response to criticism that the tests were n't an accurate reflection of ' real world ' driving , Europe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Procedure ( WLTP ) . It runs for 30 minutes , includes mixed dynamic phases that forces multiple changes of gearshift points , and factors in the influence of optional equipment ( such as wider tyres ) . There 's no word yet if it will be mirrored here , though . <p> And what of those other nasty emissions ? Well , think of the ash left after a bonfire -- following that carefully-crafted combustion process , different fuels will leave different residual matter . This includes a mix of carbon monoxide ( CO ) , oxides of nitrogen ( NOx ) , volatile organic compounds ( VOCs ) , particulate matter ( PM ) , and sulphur dioxide . <p> Exposure to CO can interfere with the blood 's capacity to carry oxygen and lead to cardiovascular disease ; VOCs include aromatics or olefins , benzene and butadiene , leading to nose and eye irritations , and headaches , all the way to liver , kidney and central nervous system damage , and cancer . Meanwhile NOx is a core contributor to smog and it irritates respiratory systems @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ do sulphur oxides that also is a precursor to acid rain ; while PM penetrates deep into the lungs , contributing to respiratory illness and cardiovascular cancer . <p> The federal government found that even in 2011 these issues contributed to the premature death of 2549 Australians -- more than the national road toll . A 2013 study showed that 9.0 per cent of heart disease deaths were due to inhaling particulate matter , while in urban areas vehicles contributed up to 70 per cent of NOx . It is these that new emissions standards are most focused on lowering , but Australia is pinned to Euro V regulations -- not Euro VI . <h> What is Euro V and Euro VI ? <p> Euro V mandates that petrol and diesel passenger cars must emit no more than 60 and 180 milligrams NOx per kilometre driven ( mg/km ) respectively , but light-commercial vehicles ( LCVs ) are permitted 82 and 280 mg/km respectively . In essence , a diesel HiLux can legally produce four times the NOx of a Camry Hybrid , though in reality it can be a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ute and just 1.6 mg/km of NOx for the hybrid . <p> But the engine is only one part of the mix . Australia 's unleaded is among the dirtiest in the world , rating 70th out 100 countries , with 150 parts per million ( ppm ) of sulphur ( see oxides problems above ) the mandate for 91RON unleaded and 50ppm for premium -- compared with 10ppm in Europe , while the mix of aromatics that cause VOCs is currently at 45 per cent compared with 35 per cent overseas . <p> By the federal government 's own modelling it believes phasing out regular unleaded and fully harmonising with the above would decrease NOx , VOC and CO emissions from motor vehicles by 22 per cent in 2022 and 29 per cent in 2030 , saving lives and providing up to $3.1 billion in health savings . <p> But requirements for upgrades to Australia 's four oil refineries -- two in Victoria at Altona by Mobil and Geelong by Viva , Lyton in Queensland by Caltex and Kwinana in Western Australia by BP -- mean they have resisted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the European Union will add 2.3 cents per litre ( cpl ) to the price of unleaded , deeming it the least cost effective option of others that include retaining 91RON but with 10ppm sulphur . Read the above health issues created by vehicles post-combustion , though -- does 2.3cpl sound worth it to you ? 
@@50085626 <p> Research into the future of Australia 's " other reef " -- the Great Southern Reef -- shows that even under the most optimistic carbon emission scenarios , ocean warming is likely to cause substantial loss of critical habitat-forming seaweeds by 2100 . <p> The research , by UWA Oceans Institute Associate Professor Thomas Wernberg and a team of international and Australian colleagues , was published today in Diversity and Distributions . The Great Southern Reef is a massive series of reefs with extensive kelp seaweed forests that extend around Australia 's southern coastline , covering around 71,000sqkm from Brisbane to Kalbarri . <p> Professor Wernberg said that over the next 85 years our temperate coastlines were likely to experience substantial reductions of habitat-forming seaweeds , which are the biological engine of the Great Southern Reef . <p> " We looked at the present and future distribution of 15 large dominant seaweed species and found they would lose between 30-100 per cent of their current area to ocean warming even under the optimistic most scenario where we aim to limit global warming to less than 2C , " Professor Wernberg said . <p> " This is bad news @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ important recreational and commercial fisheries such as abalone and rock lobster , Australia 's most valuable fisheries . " <p> All but two of the 15 species were predicted to contract southwards before 2100 . Currently dominant species such as common kelp and strapweed were predicted to lose nearly half of their present distribution to become compressed in pockets on the south coast . Other seaweeds such as giant kelp , bull kelp and crayweed were predicted to become extinct from the Australian continent . <p> Professor Wernberg said it was well known how climate change was causing ocean temperatures to increase in many regions . This was a problem for cool-water species such as temperate seaweeds and they would shift their distribution into cooler waters as a consequence , he said . <p> Co-author Dr Ben Radford , an ecological modeller with the Australian Institute of Marine Science , said there was a very strong relationship between ocean temperature and the presence of different species . <p> " By determining this relationship , and combining it with projections of future ocean temperatures from climate models , it is possible @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or not in the future , " Dr Radford said . <p> Professor Wernberg said the socio-economic as well as ecological consequences of these reductions of habitat-forming seaweeds could be devastating . <p> " These seaweeds are the trees of the oceans and the foundation of kelp forests that support ecosystem services such as biodiversity and fisheries resources worth more than $10 billion per year in Australia , " he said . <p> " In response , our research focus is now changing from documenting kelp loss to discovering solutions to increase seaweed resilience and improve restoration of impacted kelp forests . These active solutions are the only way forward if we want to maintain these unique and valuable ecosystems . " <p> Image caption : The common kelp is currently a dominant seaweed in kelp forests across the Great Southern Reef . It is predicted to lose almost half of its current distribution to ocean warming before 2100 ( Image credit : T. Wernberg ) .
